claim: Activation of the quadriceps muscles vastus lateralis (VL) and vastus medialis (VM) in the rat produces very similar forces at the distal tibia and so will produce similar joint torques.
source: Activation of the quadriceps muscles vastus lateralis (VL) and vastus medialis (VM) in the rat produces very similar forces at the distal tibia and so will produce similar joint torques (Sandercock et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sandercock et al., 2018.

claim: VL and VM have redundant contributions to task performance.
source: These muscles therefore have redundant contributions to task performance.
evidence: This is inferred from the previous statement about VL and VM producing similar joint torques, which is supported by citation.

claim: VL and VM produce opposing mediolateral forces on the patella.
source: On the other hand, VL and VM produce opposing mediolateral forces on the patella (Sandercock et al., 2018; Lin et al., 2004; Wilson and Sheehan, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sandercock et al., 2018; Lin et al., 2004; Wilson and Sheehan, 2010.

claim: In the rat, mediolateral patellar forces are not transmitted to the tibia but are balanced by contact forces between the patella and the femur within the trochlear groove.
source: In the rat, these mediolateral patellar forces are not transmitted to the tibia but are balanced by contact forces between the patella and the femur within the trochlear groove (Sandercock et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sandercock et al., 2018.

claim: Cutting the branch of the quadriceps nerve innervating VL abolished the large majority of VL activation during locomotion.
source: Cutting the branch of the quadriceps nerve innervating VL abolished the large majority of VL activation during locomotion, as illustrated in Figure 2a–b.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a-b.

claim: The loss of VL EMG persisted over the 7 week adaptation period, demonstrating the absence of VL reinnervation.
source: The loss of EMG persisted over the 7 week adaptation period, demonstrating the absence of VL reinnervation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the persistent loss of EMG activity observed in the experimental data.

claim: The mass of the denervated VL measured at the end of the experiment (i.e. 8 weeks after nerve cut) was significantly lower (p<0.001) than the mass of the intact contralateral VL.
source: Consistent with this loss of activation, the mass of the denervated VL measured at the end of the experiment (i.e. 8 weeks after nerve cut) was significantly lower (p<0.001) than the mass of the intact contralateral VL (Figure 2c), reflecting atrophy of the paralyzed muscle.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c with statistical significance p<0.001.

claim: The reduced mass of denervated VL reflects atrophy of the paralyzed muscle.
source: Consistent with this loss of activation, the mass of the denervated VL measured at the end of the experiment (i.e. 8 weeks after nerve cut) was significantly lower (p<0.001) than the mass of the intact contralateral VL (Figure 2c), reflecting atrophy of the paralyzed muscle.
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge that denervated muscles undergo atrophy.

claim: In the first week after VL nerve cut, there was a large increase of the activation of both RF and VM during stance.
source: In the first week after nerve cut, there was a large increase of the activation of both RF and VM during stance.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: By 7 weeks after the nerve cut, the activation of VM during stance returned to levels similar to those observed in baseline conditions.
source: By 7 weeks after the nerve cut, the activation of VM during stance returned to levels similar to those observed in baseline conditions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: At 7 weeks after VL nerve cut, the activation of RF remained elevated as compared to baseline conditions.
source: At this same time point, however, the activation of RF remained elevated as compared to baseline conditions, consistent with our predictions based on the neural control of internal joint stresses.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: VM activity was not significantly different from baseline at any time after VL nerve cut (pweek1 = 1, pweek2 = 1, pweek7 = 0.154).
source: While the activity of VM was not significantly different from baseline at any time after VL nerve cut (pweek1 = 1, pweek2 = 1, pweek7 = 0.154), RF activity was significantly increased at all time points (pweek1 = 0.007, pweek2 < 0.001, pweek7 < 0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: RF activity was significantly increased at all time points after VL nerve cut (pweek1 = 0.007, pweek2 < 0.001, pweek7 < 0.001).
source: While the activity of VM was not significantly different from baseline at any time after VL nerve cut (pweek1 = 1, pweek2 = 1, pweek7 = 0.154), RF activity was significantly increased at all time points (pweek1 = 0.007, pweek2 < 0.001, pweek7 < 0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The change in RF activation was significantly larger than the change in VM activation at all time points after VL nerve cut (pweek1 < 0.001, pweek2 < 0.001, pweek7 < 0.001).
source: More importantly, the change in RF activation was significantly larger than the change in VM activation at all time points (pweek1 < 0.001, pweek2 < 0.001, pweek7 < 0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There was a significant increase in RF muscle mass in the affected limb as compared to the mass of RF in the unaffected limb (p=0.047).
source: We found that there was a significant increase in RF muscle mass in the affected limb as compared to the mass of RF in the unaffected limb (p=0.047).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 with statistical significance p=0.047.

claim: The masses of VM and VI were not significantly different between the affected and unaffected limbs (VM: p=1; VI: p=1).
source: In contrast, the masses of VM and VI were not significantly different between the two limbs (VM: p=1; VI: p=1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 with statistical analysis.

claim: VL paralysis caused an initial reduction in the stance phase duration.
source: There was an initial reduction in the stance phase duration and in the range of motion at the knee, consistent with the reduction of knee extensor torque during stance caused by VL paralysis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: VL paralysis caused an initial reduction in the range of motion at the knee.
source: There was an initial reduction in the stance phase duration and in the range of motion at the knee, consistent with the reduction of knee extensor torque during stance caused by VL paralysis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The range of motion at the ankle increased after VL paralysis.
source: The range of motion at the ankle, on the other hand, increased.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The duration of the stance phase was significantly reduced in the first week after VL paralysis (pweek1 <0.001).
source: The duration of the stance phase, expressed as a percentage of the entire gait cycle, was significantly reduced in the first week after VL paralysis (pweek1 <0.001), but at later time points returned to levels that were not significantly different from baseline (pweek2 = 0.457; pweek7 = 0.192).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: At later time points (week 2 and week 7), stance phase duration returned to levels that were not significantly different from baseline (pweek2 = 0.457; pweek7 = 0.192).
source: The duration of the stance phase, expressed as a percentage of the entire gait cycle, was significantly reduced in the first week after VL paralysis (pweek1 <0.001), but at later time points returned to levels that were not significantly different from baseline (pweek2 = 0.457; pweek7 = 0.192).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The ranges of motion of the hip and knee were significantly smaller in the first week after VL paralysis (hip: pweek1 = 0.008; knee: pweek1 <0.001).
source: The ranges of motion of the hip and knee were significantly smaller in the first week after VL paralysis (hip: pweek1 = 0.008; knee: pweek1 <0.001), while the range of motion at the ankle was significantly larger (pweek1 <0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The range of motion at the ankle was significantly larger in the first week after VL paralysis (pweek1 <0.001).
source: The ranges of motion of the hip and knee were significantly smaller in the first week after VL paralysis (hip: pweek1 = 0.008; knee: pweek1 <0.001), while the range of motion at the ankle was significantly larger (pweek1 <0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: At week 2, the hip and the knee ROM remained significantly lower than baseline (hip: pweek2 = 0.007; knee: pweek2 <0.001) whereas the ankle was no longer significantly increased (pweek2 = 0.059).
source: At week 2, the hip and the knee ROM remained significantly lower than baseline (hip: pweek2 = 0.007; knee: pweek2 <0.001) whereas the ankle was no longer significantly increased (pweek2 = 0.059).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: By week 7, the ROM of the hip and ankle joints were not significantly different from baseline (hip: pweek7 = 0.502; ankle: pweek7 = 0.781) but there was a modest, though significant, decrease in the knee range of motion (pweek7 = 0.009).
source: By week 7, the ROM of the hip and ankle joints were not significantly different from baseline (hip: pweek7 = 0.502; ankle: pweek7 = 0.781) but there was a modest, though significant, decrease in the knee range of motion (pweek7 = 0.009).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The hip angle was significantly decreased after the first week (i.e. more flexed; pweek1 = 1, pweek2 = 0.003, pweek7 = 0.032).
source: As illustrated in Figure 6a–b, the hip angle was significantly decreased after the first week (i.e. more flexed; pweek1 = 1, pweek2 = 0.003, pweek7 = 0.032), and the ankle angle was significantly increased at all time points (i.e. more extended; pweek1 = 0.030, pweek2 = 0.004, pweek7 = 0.038) as compared to baseline.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 6a-b.

claim: The ankle angle was significantly increased at all time points (i.e. more extended; pweek1 = 0.030, pweek2 = 0.004, pweek7 = 0.038) as compared to baseline.
source: As illustrated in Figure 6a–b, the hip angle was significantly decreased after the first week (i.e. more flexed; pweek1 = 1, pweek2 = 0.003, pweek7 = 0.032), and the ankle angle was significantly increased at all time points (i.e. more extended; pweek1 = 0.030, pweek2 = 0.004, pweek7 = 0.038) as compared to baseline.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 6a-b.

claim: The knee angle was significantly reduced in the first two weeks after VL paralysis (pweek1 <0.001, pweek2 = 0.031), but was not significantly different from baseline at 7 weeks (pweek7 = 0.167).
source: On the other hand, although the knee angle was significantly reduced in the first two weeks after VL paralysis (pweek1 <0.001, pweek2 = 0.031), it was not significantly different from baseline at 7 weeks (pweek7 = 0.167).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Both limb length and limb angle measured at the end of stance were initially altered after VL paralysis (limb length: pweek1 <0.001; limb angle: pweek1 = 0.002).
source: As illustrated in Figure 6c, both limb length and limb angle measured at the end of stance were initially altered after VL paralysis (limb length: pweek1 <0.001; limb angle: pweek1 = 0.002).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Limb length and limb angle alterations disappeared over the adaptation period so that these measures were not significantly different from baseline levels (limb length: pweek2 = 0.142, pweek7 = 1; limb angle: pweek2 = 0.141, pweek7 = 1).
source: However, these alterations disappeared over the adaptation period so that these measures were not significantly different from baseline levels (limb length: pweek2 = 0.142, pweek7 = 1; limb angle: pweek2 = 0.141, pweek7 = 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Animals compensated for VL paralysis by increasing activation of RF while maintaining the activation of VM at levels similar to those observed before the perturbation.
source: We found that animals compensated for VL paralysis by increasing activation of RF while maintaining the activation of VM at levels similar to those observed before the perturbation.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The increased RF activation strategy restores the knee extension torque lost after VL paralysis while causing minimal additional mediolateral patellar forces.
source: This strategy restores the knee extension torque lost after VL paralysis while causing minimal additional mediolateral patellar forces.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known mechanical properties of RF and the experimental observations.

claim: The increased RF activation resulted in a persistent perturbation in joint kinematics due to the extra hip flexor torque from RF.
source: The increased RF activation resulted in a persistent perturbation in joint kinematics due to the extra hip flexor torque from RF, but global aspects of limb kinematics were restored.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Global aspects of limb kinematics were restored after VL paralysis.
source: The increased RF activation resulted in a persistent perturbation in joint kinematics due to the extra hip flexor torque from RF, but global aspects of limb kinematics were restored.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: The CNS considers internal joint stresses and strains when choosing muscle activations.
source: These results suggest that the CNS considers internal joint stresses and strains when choosing muscle activations.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing preferential increase in RF activation.

claim: Increased activation of RF introduces an additional flexion torque at the hip.
source: In contrast, increased activation of RF, while restoring the knee extension torque lost by VL paralysis, also introduces an additional flexion torque at the hip (Johnson et al., 2008; Greene, 1963) (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Johnson et al., 2008 and Greene, 1963, and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Increasing activation of RF restores knee extension function while producing negligible additional mediolateral forces on the patella.
source: Increasing activation of RF restores knee extension function while producing negligible additional mediolateral forces on the patella (Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on the known mechanical properties of RF illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Higher activation of VM would increase the medial force on the patella and cause excess patellofemoral loading.
source: On the other hand, higher activation of VM would increase the medial force on the patella and cause excess patellofemoral loading.
evidence: This is based on the known mechanical properties of VM and inference about the consequences of increased activation.

claim: The selective increase in RF mass likely reflects a use-dependent strengthening of that muscle.
source: We also observed a selective increase in the mass of RF that likely reflects a use-dependent strengthening of that muscle, although we did not confirm this by measuring peak forces or myosin content (Blaauw et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about use-dependent muscle adaptation, with a citation to Blaauw et al., 2013.

claim: The increased RF mass suggests that at late time points of the adaptation, the loss of VL was compensated both by higher neural activity and by additional force generating capability of RF.
source: Furthermore, it suggests that at late time points of the adaptation, the loss of VL was compensated both by higher neural activity and by additional force generating capability of RF.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed increase in RF mass and activation.

claim: The increased RF activation was not specific to treadmill locomotion, but was also used in behaviors not measured in the study.
source: Finally, this result suggests that the increased RF activation was not specific to treadmill locomotion, but was also used in behaviors we did not measure here; if there was increased VM or VI activation in other behaviors, we would have observed an increase in the mass of those muscles.
evidence: This is an inference based on the selective increase in RF mass and the absence of mass increase in VM and VI.

claim: There was no consistent change in the activation of VI during the adaptation period.
source: The observation of no change in the mass of VI also suggests that there was no consistent change in the activation of this muscle during the adaptation period, though we did not record from VI in these experiments due its small size and inaccessibility for implantation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of mass change in VI.

claim: VM activation levels were on average similar to those observed before VL paralysis, even after 7 weeks of adaptation.
source: We did not observe a complete silencing of VM, even after 7 weeks of adaptation: VM activation levels were on average similar to those observed before VL paralysis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: A residual medial force on the patella persisted throughout the adaptation period.
source: This implies that a residual medial force on the patella persisted throughout the adaptation period.
evidence: This is an inference based on the persistent VM activation and the known mechanical properties of VM.

claim: Residual VM activity might reflect a compromise between unbalanced mediolateral patellar forces and perturbations in joint kinematics caused by the increased activation of RF.
source: Such residual VM activity might reflect a compromise between unbalanced mediolateral patellar forces and perturbations in joint kinematics caused by the increased activation of RF.
evidence: This is speculation about the possible explanation for the observed residual VM activity.

claim: Muscle paralysis caused persistent changes at individual joint kinematics.
source: Although muscle paralysis caused persistent changes at individual joint kinematics, we observed restoration of global limb kinematics.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Global limb kinematics were restored after VL paralysis.
source: Although muscle paralysis caused persistent changes at individual joint kinematics, we observed restoration of global limb kinematics.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: The results are consistent with ideas such as those used in uncontrolled manifold analyses.
source: This result is consistent with ideas such as those used in uncontrolled manifold analyses (Latash et al., 2007) and with previous results examining adaptation following paralysis of triceps surae in rats and cats (Chang et al., 2009; Bauman and Chang, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Latash et al., 2007; Chang et al., 2009; Bauman and Chang, 2013.

claim: The results suggest a hierarchical control of movement, in which higher level variables related to task goals (i.e. global limb variables) are preserved after VL paralysis while lower level variables related to task execution (i.e. individual joint angles) are allowed to vary.
source: In this context, our results suggest a hierarchical control of movement, in which higher level variables related to task goals (i.e. global limb variables) are preserved after VL paralysis while lower level variables related to task execution (i.e. individual joint angles) are allowed to vary.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations of restored global kinematics but persistent changes in individual joint angles.

claim: Many criteria have been proposed to influence the activation of muscles during behavior, but they generally do not consider the internal state of joints.
source: Many criteria have been proposed to influence the activation of muscles during behavior (Alessandro, 2016; Prilutsky, 2000), but they generally do not consider the internal state of joints.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Alessandro, 2016 and Prilutsky, 2000.

claim: Some criteria might indirectly minimize joint stresses and strains (e.g. minimum jerk or torque change), but they would not predict the selective increase in RF activation observed in this study.
source: Although some of these criteria might indirectly minimize joint stresses and strains (e.g. minimum jerk [Flash and Hogan, 1985] or torque change [Uno et al., 1989]), they would not predict the selective increase in RF activation observed here.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known properties of these optimization criteria, with citations to Flash and Hogan, 1985 and Uno et al., 1989.

claim: Including criteria that explicitly consider the consequences of muscle activation on joint stresses and strains might improve the predictions of optimization approaches.
source: Including criteria that explicitly consider the consequences of muscle activation on joint stresses and strains might improve the predictions of such optimization approaches.
evidence: This is speculation about how to improve motor control models.

claim: The co-evolution of neural control and musculoskeletal anatomy might result in a neuromechanical system such that muscle activations optimizing task performance criteria also optimize internal joint state criteria.
source: The co-evolution of neural control and musculoskeletal anatomy (Valero-Cuevas, 2015) might result in a neuromechanical system such that muscle activations optimizing task performance criteria also optimize internal joint state criteria.
evidence: This is speculation about evolutionary mechanisms, with a citation to Valero-Cuevas, 2015.

claim: When VM and VL are intact, a criterion that minimizes muscle metabolism or that considers signal dependent variability would predict a distributed activation of VM and VL.
source: For example, when VM and VL are intact, a criterion that minimizes muscle metabolism (Kistemaker et al., 2014; Prilutsky, 2000), or that considers signal dependent variability (Harris and Wolpert, 1998; Haruno and Wolpert, 2005) would predict a distributed activation of VM and VL.
evidence: This is an inference based on established motor control theories, with citations to Kistemaker et al., 2014; Prilutsky, 2000; Harris and Wolpert, 1998; Haruno and Wolpert, 2005.

claim: Distributed activation of VM and VL might result from optimization over evolutionary time scales and be implemented in coordinative structures such as muscle synergies within the spinal cord or other brain regions.
source: This distributed activation of VM and VL might result from optimization over evolutionary time scales (Giszter, 2015) and be implemented in coordinative structures such as muscle synergies (Tresch and Jarc, 2009; Alessandro et al., 2013a; Alessandro et al., 2013b) within the spinal cord (Levine et al., 2014; Hart and Giszter, 2010; Takei et al., 2017) or other brain regions (Overduin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculation about evolutionary and neural mechanisms, with multiple citations.

claim: Distributed activation of VM and VL could balance net mediolateral patellar forces, even though such a balance was not explicitly considered.
source: This distributed activation could in turn balance net mediolateral patellar forces, even though such a balance was not explicitly considered.
evidence: This is speculation about how implicit regulation might occur.

claim: After injuries that alter limb properties, implicit regulation of internal joint state might be compromised.
source: After injuries that alter limb properties (Gutierrez et al., 2009; O'Connor et al., 1993), this implicit regulation of internal joint state might be compromised (Needle et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculation based on citations to Gutierrez et al., 2009; O'Connor et al., 1993; Needle et al., 2014.

claim: After injuries, the CNS might be forced into a solution that requires a tradeoff between task performance and internal joint stresses and strains.
source: In these situations, the CNS might be forced into a solution that requires a tradeoff between task performance and internal joint stresses and strains, such as that observed in our experiments.
evidence: This is speculation about the consequences of injury, based on the experimental observations.

claim: One common suggestion is that patellofemoral pain (PFP) results from an imbalance in mediolateral patellar forces.
source: Although many factors have been shown to contribute to PFP (Smith et al., 2018; Fagan and Delahunt, 2008), one common suggestion is that PFP results from an imbalance in mediolateral patellar forces (Pal et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Smith et al., 2018; Fagan and Delahunt, 2008; Pal et al., 2012.

claim: The CNS regulates mediolateral patellar forces, but this regulation is imperfect since VM activation persisted after VL paralysis.
source: Our results show that although the CNS regulates these mediolateral forces, this regulation is imperfect since VM activation persisted after VL paralysis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observation of persistent VM activation.

claim: PFP might result from imperfect regulation of patellar forces, potentially reflecting a compromise between criteria related to task performance and internal joint states.
source: PFP might result from similarly imperfect regulation of patellar forces, potentially reflecting a compromise between criteria related to task performance and internal joint states.
evidence: This is speculation about the etiology of PFP based on the experimental findings.

claim: The experiments highlight the importance of considering the consequences of rehabilitation on internal joint stresses and strains following injuries, rather than solely focusing on restoration of task performance.
source: More broadly, our experiments highlight the importance of considering the consequences of rehabilitation on internal joint stresses and strains following injuries (Farrokhi et al., 2013; Shull et al., 2013; Simic et al., 2011), rather than solely focusing on restoration of task performance (Hollands et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference about clinical implications, with citations to Farrokhi et al., 2013; Shull et al., 2013; Simic et al., 2011; Hollands et al., 2012.

claim: Sensory receptors in the joint can convey information about strains in ligaments or stresses between bones.
source: Sensory receptors in the joint can convey information about strains in ligaments or stresses between bones.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about joint sensory receptors.

claim: Activity in joint sensory receptors can be conveyed to spinal interneuronal populations and other areas to drive rapid feedback control of muscles or longer term adaptation of muscle activations.
source: Activity in these receptors can be conveyed to spinal interneuronal populations (Solomonow et al., 1987; Iles et al., 1990) and other areas (Sjölander et al., 2002) to drive rapid feedback control of muscles (Ferrell, 1980) or longer term adaptation of muscle activations in order to avoid potential injury.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Solomonow et al., 1987; Iles et al., 1990; Sjölander et al., 2002; Ferrell, 1980.

claim: The CNS could derive information about internal joint structures indirectly from muscle proprioceptors, combining information about muscle forces and lengths with 'internal' models of muscle anatomy to estimate joint stresses and strains.
source: The CNS could also derive information about internal joint structures indirectly from muscle proprioceptors (Wilmink and Nichols, 2003), combining information about muscle forces and lengths with 'internal' models of muscle anatomy to estimate joint stresses and strains.
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms, with a citation to Wilmink and Nichols, 2003.

claim: Predictive models of muscle actions, combined with efference copy of motor commands, could be used to make feedforward predictions of internal joint stresses and strains.
source: Similarly, predictive models of muscle actions, combined with efference copy of motor commands, could be used to make feedforward predictions of internal joint stresses and strains.
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms.

claim: The strong coherence between VM and VL across frequencies observed in humans is consistent with the importance of coordinated activation of these muscles.
source: The strong coherence between VM and VL across frequencies (Laine et al., 2015) observed in humans is consistent with the importance of coordinated activation of these muscles (Brøchner Nielsen et al., 2017), whether by feedforward or feedback processes.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Laine et al., 2015 and Brøchner Nielsen et al., 2017.

claim: Coordinated muscle activation is similar to ideas of muscle synergies, so that the balanced activation of muscles within a synergy would reflect regulation of joint stresses and strains.
source: This coordinated muscle activation is also similar to ideas of muscle synergies (Tresch and Jarc, 2009; Alessandro et al., 2013a; Alessandro et al., 2013b), so that the balanced activation of muscles within a synergy would reflect regulation of joint stresses and strains.
evidence: This is speculation about the relationship between muscle synergies and joint stress regulation, with citations to Tresch and Jarc, 2009; Alessandro et al., 2013a; Alessandro et al., 2013b.

claim: Neural control of internal joint states might be relatively coarse, only responding to large deviations in joint states inducing discomfort or pain.
source: Note that neural control of internal joint states might be relatively coarse, only responding to large deviations in joint states inducing discomfort or pain (Grigg and Greenspan, 1977).
evidence: This is speculation with a citation to Grigg and Greenspan, 1977.

claim: Coarse control of joint state might reflect the 'good enough' habitual strategy, potentially resulting in the residual activation of VM observed in the experiments.
source: Such a coarse control of joint state might reflect the 'good enough' habitual strategy (de Rugy et al., 2012) described above, potentially resulting in the residual activation of VM observed in our experiments.
evidence: This is speculation with a citation to de Rugy et al., 2012.

claim: The loss of sensory information from the paralyzed muscle might contribute to the observed changes in muscle activation.
source: Although the muscle paralysis by denervation used in these experiments has been used in many studies to examine neural adaptation strategies (Bauman and Chang, 2013; Dambreville et al., 2016; Frigon and Rossignol, 2007; Bennett et al., 2012; Bouyer et al., 2001; Maas et al., 2007), the loss of sensory information from the paralyzed muscle might contribute to the observed changes in muscle activation (Akay et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculation about a potential confound, with multiple citations.

claim: The rat knee joint might provide a tractable experimental model to examine the neural control of joint stresses and strains in both healthy subjects and following injury.
source: The rat knee joint might therefore provide a tractable experimental model to examine the neural control of joint stresses and strains in both healthy subjects and following injury.
evidence: This is speculation about the utility of the rat model based on the experimental findings.

claim: Experiments were performed on female Sprague Dawley rats (n = 6).
source: We performed experiments on female Sprague Dawley rats (n = 6).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental subjects.

claim: All procedures were approved by the Animal Care Committee of Northwestern University.
source: All the procedures were approved by the Animal Care Committee of Northwestern University.
evidence: This is a direct statement about ethical approval.

claim: Chronic EMG electrodes were implanted in multiple hindlimb muscles including VL, VM, RF, SM, BFp, TA, and GRc.
source: We implanted pairs of electrodes in seven muscles: vastus lateralis (VL), vastus medialis (VM), rectus femoris (RF), semimembranosus (SM), biceps femoris posterior (BFp), tibialis anterior (TA), and caudal gracilis (GRc).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental methods.

claim: During VL paralysis surgery, the quadriceps nerve plexus was exposed, the branch to VL was isolated, anesthetized with lidocaine, tied off in two locations with silk suture, and then cut between the sutures.
source: During aseptic surgery (isoflurane, 3% in O2 ~ 2 l/min), we exposed the quadriceps nerve plexus, and isolated the branch to VL. We anesthetized this branch with lidocaine, tied it off in two locations with silk suture to prevent re-innervation, and then cut between the sutures.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental methods.

claim: Each recording session consisted of two minutes of locomotion at the maximum comfortable speed (12–15 m/min) and incline (usually +25%).
source: Each recording session consisted of two minutes of locomotion at the maximum comfortable speed (12–15 m/min) and incline (usually +25%) to induce strong quadriceps activations.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental protocol.

claim: The 3D position of markers was tracked using a motion capture system (Vicon) at a frequency of 200 Hz.
source: The 3D position of markers was tracked using a motion capture system (Vicon) at a frequency of 200 Hz.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data acquisition methods.

claim: Kinematic signals were low-pass filtered offline at a cut-off frequency of 10 Hz (5th order Butterworth).
source: These signals were low-pass filtered offline at a cut-off frequency of 10 Hz (5th order Butterworth).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data processing methods.

claim: The 3D position of the knee was estimated by triangulation, using the lengths of the femur and the tibia, to reduce errors due to differential movements of the skin.
source: In order to reduce errors due to differential movements of the skin (Filipe et al., 2006; Bauman and Chang, 2010), we estimated the 3D position of the knee by triangulation, using the lengths of the femur and the tibia (Bauman and Chang, 2010).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data processing methods, with citations to Filipe et al., 2006 and Bauman and Chang, 2010.

claim: Differential EMG signals were amplified (1000X), band-pass filtered (30–1000 Hz) and notch filtered (60 Hz), and then digitalized (5000 Hz).
source: Differential EMG signals were amplified (1000X), band-pass filtered (30–1000 Hz) and notch filtered (60 Hz), and then digitalized (5000 Hz).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data acquisition methods.

claim: The digitalized EMG signals were further band-pass filtered offline to remove motion artifacts (5–500 Hz, 4th order Butterworth), rectified, and envelopes were computed from the rectified signals.
source: The digitalized signals were further band-pass filtered offline to remove motion artifacts (5–500 Hz, 4th order Butterworth), rectified, and envelopes were computed from the rectified signals.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data processing methods.

claim: Linear Mixed Effect Models (LMEM) were employed to analyze both kinematic and EMG data using the nlme package in the R environment.
source: We employed Linear Mixed Effect Models (LMEM) to analyze both kinematic and EMG data using the nlme package (Pinheiro et al., 2017) in the R environment.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the statistical methods, with a citation to Pinheiro et al., 2017.

claim: The use of LMEMs allows exploitation of large numbers of observations for each animal across the adaptation period, obtaining maximal statistical power from a relatively small number of animals.
source: The use of LMEMs allows us to exploit the fact that we have large numbers of observations for each animal across the adaptation period, obtaining the maximal statistical power from a relatively small number of animals.
evidence: This is a statement about the rationale for the statistical approach.

claim: LMEMs allow analysis of samples of different size, coping with missing data, and taking into account variability at different levels of the dataset.
source: LMEMs also allow us to analyze samples of different size (e.g. unequal numbers of strides across days and animals), to cope with missing data (potentially due to the inclusion criteria described above), and to take into account variability at different levels of the dataset (e.g. across strides, across days, and across subjects).
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of the statistical approach.

claim: Tests were considered statistically significant if their p-values were lower than the 0.05 significance level.
source: We considered tests to be statistically significant if their p-values were lower than the 0.05 significance level.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the statistical criteria.

claim: To compare the masses of the quadriceps in the denervated limb to those in the intact limb, paired t-tests were performed for each muscle, and the obtained p-values were adjusted with Bonferroni corrections.
source: To compare the masses of the quadriceps in the denervated limb to those in the intact limb, we performed paired t-tests for each muscle, and we adjusted the obtained p-values with Bonferroni corrections.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the statistical methods.

claim: Muscles must act through joints to produce movements.
source: In order to produce movements, muscles must act through joints.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of biomechanics.

claim: The translation from muscle force to limb movement is mediated by internal joint structures that permit movement in some directions but constrain it in others.
source: The translation from muscle force to limb movement is mediated by internal joint structures that permit movement in some directions but constrain it in others.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of joint mechanics.

claim: Muscle forces acting against constrained directions will not affect limb movements.
source: Although muscle forces acting against constrained directions will not affect limb movements, such forces can cause excess stresses and strains in joint structures, leading to pain or injury.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of joint mechanics.

claim: Muscle forces acting against constrained directions can cause excess stresses and strains in joint structures, leading to pain or injury.
source: Although muscle forces acting against constrained directions will not affect limb movements, such forces can cause excess stresses and strains in joint structures, leading to pain or injury.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of joint mechanics and clinical observations.

claim: The CNS chooses muscle activations to avoid excessive joint stresses and strains.
source: In this study, we hypothesized that the central nervous system (CNS) chooses muscle activations to avoid excessive joint stresses and strains.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis of the study.

claim: The CNS compromises between restoration of task performance and regulation of joint stresses and strains.
source: We show that the CNS compromises between restoration of task performance and regulation of joint stresses and strains.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding, supported by experimental data.

claim: Common theories emphasizing task performance are insufficient to explain muscle activations during behaviors.
source: These results have significant implications to our understanding of the neural control of movements, suggesting that common theories emphasizing task performance are insufficient to explain muscle activations during behaviors.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The question of how the CNS determines motor commands is usually answered in terms of task performance.
source: The question of how the central nervous system (CNS) determines motor commands is usually answered in terms of task performance (Todorov and Jordan, 2002; Guigon et al., 2007; Scott, 2004): the CNS activates muscles according to how they contribute to task goals such as grasping an object or escaping a predator.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Todorov and Jordan, 2002; Guigon et al., 2007; Scott, 2004.

claim: Additional criteria based on energetics, dynamics, or kinematics can further constrain muscle activations.
source: Additional criteria based on energetics (Todorov and Jordan, 2002; Izawa et al., 2008; Kurtzer et al., 2006), dynamics (Uno et al., 1989), or kinematics (Flash and Hogan, 1985) can further constrain muscle activations, and the specific criteria used by the CNS to specify muscle activations underlying behavior has been the topic of considerable research (Scott, 2004; Todorov, 2004; Alessandro, 2016; Kistemaker et al., 2014; Prilutsky, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Previous work on motor control has generally ignored how muscles act on internal joint structures such as ligaments or articular cartilage between bones.
source: This previous work, however, has generally ignored another critical aspect of muscle actions: how muscles act on internal joint structures such as ligaments or articular cartilage between bones (Herzog et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Herzog et al., 2003.

claim: Muscle actions on internal joint structures have been considered in clinical biomechanics or sports medicine in the context of injuries.
source: Although muscle actions on internal joint structures have been considered in clinical biomechanics or sports medicine in the context of injuries (Farrokhi et al., 2013; Pal et al., 2012; Felson, 2013; Konrath et al., 2017), their more general role in the context of the neural control of movement and how they are balanced with task goals remains poorly understood.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Farrokhi et al., 2013; Pal et al., 2012; Felson, 2013; Konrath et al., 2017.

claim: The more general role of muscle actions on internal joint structures in the context of neural control of movement and how they are balanced with task goals remains poorly understood.
source: Although muscle actions on internal joint structures have been considered in clinical biomechanics or sports medicine in the context of injuries (Farrokhi et al., 2013; Pal et al., 2012; Felson, 2013; Konrath et al., 2017), their more general role in the context of the neural control of movement and how they are balanced with task goals remains poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Evaluating whether the CNS regulates stresses and strains within internal joint structures is challenging, primarily because of the complexity of joint mechanics.
source: Evaluating whether the CNS regulates stresses and strains within internal joint structures is challenging, primarily because of the complexity of joint mechanics.
evidence: This is a statement about the challenges in studying this topic.

claim: Since muscles can only affect task performance by acting through joint structures, any manipulation affecting joint structures will usually also affect task performance.
source: Since muscles can only affect task performance by acting through joint structures (Herzog et al., 2003), any manipulation affecting joint structures will usually also affect task performance.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge with a citation to Herzog et al., 2003.

claim: Damage to a ligament will alter both the distribution of stresses and strains within the joint as well as how muscle forces are transmitted across the joint.
source: For example, damage to a ligament (Gutierrez et al., 2009; Needle et al., 2014; O'Connor et al., 1993) will alter both the distribution of stresses and strains within the joint (Chen et al., 2017; Gardinier et al., 2013) as well as how muscle forces are transmitted across the joint (Boeth et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Removal of sensory feedback from joint structures might compromise neural control of joint stresses and strains.
source: Similarly, although removal of sensory feedback from joint structures might compromise neural control of joint stresses and strains (O'Connor et al., 1993; O'Connor et al., 1992; Salo et al., 2002; Solomonow, 2006; Solomonow and Krogsgaard, 2001; Johansson et al., 1991), this sensory feedback can also provide information about task performance (Ferrell et al., 1985; Sjölander et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Sensory feedback from joint structures can provide information about task performance.
source: Similarly, although removal of sensory feedback from joint structures might compromise neural control of joint stresses and strains (O'Connor et al., 1993; O'Connor et al., 1992; Salo et al., 2002; Solomonow, 2006; Solomonow and Krogsgaard, 2001; Johansson et al., 1991), this sensory feedback can also provide information about task performance (Ferrell et al., 1985; Sjölander et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ferrell et al., 1985 and Sjölander et al., 2002.

claim: These challenges have made it difficult to reach clear conclusions as to whether the CNS controls internal joint stresses and strains.
source: These challenges have made it difficult to reach clear conclusions as to whether the CNS controls internal joint stresses and strains.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Vastus intermedius (VI) is very small in the rat and so is unlikely to contribute substantially to the adaptation following VL paralysis.
source: Note that vastus intermedius (VI) is very small in the rat and so is unlikely to contribute substantially to the adaptation following VL paralysis.
evidence: This is based on anatomical knowledge of the rat.

claim: Rats compensated for the loss of VL by preferentially increasing activation of RF.
source: Our results show that rats compensated for the loss of VL by preferentially increasing activation of RF, consistent with the hypothesis that the CNS chooses muscle activations to minimize stresses and strains to internal joint structures.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding, supported by experimental data.

claim: The preferential increase in RF activation is consistent with the hypothesis that the CNS chooses muscle activations to minimize stresses and strains to internal joint structures.
source: Our results show that rats compensated for the loss of VL by preferentially increasing activation of RF, consistent with the hypothesis that the CNS chooses muscle activations to minimize stresses and strains to internal joint structures.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.
